es: Reconocer los ganchos de apertura (anécdota, dato, promesa, pregunta) de una charla, su efecto sobre el público y las señales que anuncian la estructura.

teaching.en: A strong hook should command attention within ten seconds and set the tone for everything the speaker says afterwards.
teaching.es: Un buen gancho debe captar la atención en diez segundos y marcar el tono de todo lo que el orador diga después.
teaching.explanationEs: Command attention y set the tone describen el efecto del gancho: atrapar primero, orientar después.
segments: A strong hook should command attention within ten seconds and
set the tone for everything the speaker says afterwards.
teaching.audioText: A strong hook should command attention within ten seconds and set the tone for everything the speaker says afterwards.

teaching.en: Speakers who lead with an anecdote often strike a chord, because a personal story lets strangers recognise their own lives in it.
teaching.es: Quienes abren con una anécdota suelen conectar, porque un relato personal permite que extraños reconozcan su propia vida en él.
teaching.explanationEs: Lead with + sustantivo indica con qué se empieza; strike a chord significa conectar emocionalmente.
segments: Speakers who lead with an anecdote often strike a chord, because
a personal story lets strangers recognise their own lives in it.
teaching.audioText: Speakers who lead with an anecdote often strike a chord, because a personal story lets strangers recognise their own lives in it.

teaching.en: A single statistic can serve as an opening gambit, provided the figure is surprising and the speaker explains why it matters.
teaching.es: Un solo dato puede servir de primera jugada, siempre que la cifra sorprenda y el orador explique por qué importa.
teaching.explanationEs: Provided (that) introduce una condición: el dato funciona solo si se explica su relevancia.
segments: A single statistic can serve as an opening gambit, provided the
figure is surprising and the speaker explains why it matters.
teaching.audioText: A single statistic can serve as an opening gambit, provided the figure is surprising and the speaker explains why it matters.

teaching.en: A clear promise helps to win over the audience, since listeners stay attentive when they know what they will gain.
teaching.es: Una promesa clara ayuda a ganarse al público, ya que los oyentes siguen atentos cuando saben lo que van a obtener.
teaching.explanationEs: Win over es «persuadir, ganarse a alguien»; no lo confundas con win, que es ganar una competición.
segments: A clear promise helps to win over the audience, since
listeners stay attentive when they know what they will gain.
teaching.audioText: A clear promise helps to win over the audience, since listeners stay attentive when they know what they will gain.

teaching.en: After the hook, a signpost shows listeners where the talk is heading, and a brief outline stops them getting lost.
teaching.es: Después del gancho, una señal de organización muestra adónde va la charla, y un breve esquema evita que se pierdan.
teaching.explanationEs: La señal no aporta contenido nuevo: anuncia el camino, y por eso aparece justo tras el gancho.
segments: After the hook, a signpost shows listeners where the talk
is heading, and a brief outline stops them getting lost.
teaching.audioText: After the hook, a signpost shows listeners where the talk is heading, and a brief outline stops them getting lost.

prompt.es: Clasifica la apertura del texto según el gancho que emplea.

choices.text: It leads with a statistic meant to surprise listeners.
It leads with an anecdote meant to make listeners laugh.
It leads with a promise meant to reassure listeners.

feedback.es: La cifra («nine out of ten») y su tono inquietante son los rasgos de un dato usado como gancho.

hint.es: Busca una cifra medible: ese rasgo identifica el tipo de gancho.

origin.text: Nine out of ten people will forget most of this talk by next week, and yet we prepare our slides as if everyone will remember every word.

prompt.es: Completa: «Su primera frase debía captar la atención antes de que nadie se distrajera.»

answer.text: command

feedback.es: Command attention es la colocación que describe un gancho capaz de imponerse sobre cualquier distracción.

hint.es: Es el verbo que aparece en la colocación «___ attention».

origin.text: The speaker knew that his first sentence had to ___ attention before anyone reached for a phone. So he began with a story about a stolen bicycle.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Una primera jugada debe marcar el tono de toda la charla.»

answer.text: An opening gambit should set the tone for the whole talk

feedback.es: Set the tone + for se usa para el efecto que tiene la apertura sobre todo lo que viene después.

hint.es: El sujeto es An opening gambit; el verbo modal va justo después.

prompt.es: ¿Qué recurso usa el orador para abrir su charla?

choices.text: An anecdote about a boring talk that the speaker once sat through.
A question that asks listeners to examine their own experience of talks.
A statistic showing how few listeners remember the start of any talk.

feedback.es: La pregunta pide al público que recuerde una experiencia propia: es un gancho de pregunta con efecto personal.

origin.text: Think back to the last talk you attended. Can you remember the opening? If you cannot, you are not alone, and that is precisely the problem this morning's session sets out to solve.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige cómo describe el orador lo que ganará el público.

choices.text: He guarantees that nobody in this room will ever wait through a long delay again.
He admits that the experience taught him little and moves on.
He offers a practical benefit and signals how the talk is organised.

feedback.es: Tras la anécdota del aeropuerto, el orador promete un beneficio práctico (elegir el método) y anuncia tres formas: promesa y estructura.

origin.audio: Last winter, I slept two nights in an airport. Nobody had warned me that a long delay could teach me so much. Today, I will outline three simple ways to survive a long wait, and by the end you will know which one suits you best.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada apertura con el efecto que busca sobre el público.

pairs: What would you do if your flight vanished from the screen?

pairs.es: Obliga al público a pensar en su propia reacción

pairs: Two thirds of passengers never read the delay notice.

pairs.es: Sorprende con una cifra medible

pairs: I once spent a night on a cold airport floor.

pairs.es: Crea cercanía con un relato personal

pairs: By the end, you will have a plan for every delay.

pairs.es: Compromete al orador con un resultado

feedback.es: Cada apertura produce un efecto distinto: la pregunta hace pensar, la cifra sorprende, el relato acerca y la promesa compromete.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cómo organiza la oradora su apertura?

choices.text: A personal mistake, then a statistic, then a two-step plan.
A statistic, then a personal mistake, then a two-step plan.
A personal mistake, then a joke, then a two-step plan.

feedback.es: Primero cuenta su error (anécdota), luego da la cifra y termina anunciando dos pasos con First y Then.

origin.audio: Let me begin with an embarrassing story. Three years ago, I was on a stage very like this one, and my first slide read: Welcome, today I will talk about planning your week. Within a minute, half the room was looking at their phones. Why? Because I had opened with information, not with a reason to care. So tonight I will do it differently. Nine out of ten listeners forget a talk within a week, and I want you to be the exception. First, I will show you one mistake. Then I will give you a simple repair.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué implica que quiera que el público sea «la excepción»?

choices.text: That she doubts the figure she has just quoted is reliable.
That she hopes to make her talk memorable for everyone present.
That she will test the audience at the end of the session.

feedback.es: Al pedir que sean «la excepción», sugiere que quiere que recuerden la charla, frente a los nueve que la olvidan.

origin.audio: Let me begin with an embarrassing story. Three years ago, I was on a stage very like this one, and my first slide read: Welcome, today I will talk about planning your week. Within a minute, half the room was looking at their phones. Why? Because I had opened with information, not with a reason to care. So tonight I will do it differently. Nine out of ten listeners forget a talk within a week, and I want you to be the exception. First, I will show you one mistake. Then I will give you a simple repair.

prompt.es: Completa: «Nadie esperaba que una cifra sobre bicicletas conectara con toda la sala.»

answer.text: strike

feedback.es: Strike a chord es la colocación fija para una idea que conecta con el público; hit a chord y touch a chord son variantes aceptables.

origin.text: Nobody expected a figure about bicycles to ___ a chord with the whole room. Yet the pause that followed showed that it had.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito escribe el autor este párrafo?

choices.text: To persuade speakers to skip the thanks and begin with a joke.
To explain why audiences lose concentration once an argument gets difficult.
To challenge the habit of easing into a talk with polite remarks.

feedback.es: El autor sostiene que empezar con prudencia sale caro: el público decide en segundos y no vuelve atrás.

origin.text: Speakers are often advised to open gently, with a greeting, a thank-you and a few polite remarks. I would argue that the advice is a mistake. A cautious start may feel respectful, but it gives a bored audience no reason to stay, and by the time the real argument begins, attention has already drifted away.

prompt.es: ¿Qué actitud muestra la autora hacia las aperturas con una cifra?

choices.text: She values them only when the speaker explains why the figure matters.
She values them mainly because a surprising number is easy to remember later.
She considers them clever but less useful than a good personal anecdote.

feedback.es: Concede que la cifra sorprende, pero solo la valora si el orador explica su relevancia: una aprobación condicionada.

origin.text: A surprising figure can be a fine opening gambit, but only if the speaker tells us at once why it matters. Otherwise, the number hangs in the air like a joke without an ending, and the audience admires it briefly before forgetting it.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La señal anuncia el camino y el esquema evita que el público se pierda.»

answer.text: The signpost shows the route and the outline stops listeners getting lost

feedback.es: Signpost y outline cumplen funciones distintas: la señal indica el rumbo y el esquema da el mapa completo.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué efecto tiene la promesa de la oradora.

choices.text: It admits that the session may not deliver anything useful.
It gives tired listeners a concrete reason to stay alert.
It sets a test of how closely the audience is listening.

feedback.es: La promesa concreta y su tono de compromiso dan al público cansado un motivo para seguir atento.

origin.audio: Most of you came here tired, and I know that. So let me make you a promise: by the end of this session, you will have one technique you can use tomorrow morning. If you do not, come and find me, and I will apologise in person.

es: Ordenar y completar un discurso con señales de organización (moreover, having said that, moving on, to sum up) y preguntas retóricas que guían al público.

teaching.en: I will first explain why the problem persists; moreover, I will show what our neighbours have already done about it.
teaching.es: Primero explicaré por qué persiste el problema; además, mostraré lo que nuestros vecinos ya han hecho al respecto.
teaching.explanationEs: Moreover suma un punto más al anterior; va seguido de coma y precedido de punto y coma o de punto.
segments: I will first explain why the problem persists; moreover, I
will show what our neighbours have already done about it.
teaching.audioText: I will first explain why the problem persists; moreover, I will show what our neighbours have already done about it.

teaching.en: Having said that, let me briefly touch on the risks, and then recap the plan before moving on.
teaching.es: Dicho esto, déjame tratar brevemente los riesgos y luego recapitular el plan antes de pasar a otro punto.
teaching.explanationEs: Having said that matiza lo anterior; moving on abre otro punto; recap repasa lo que ya se dijo.
segments: Having said that, let me briefly touch on the
risks, and then recap the plan before moving on.
teaching.audioText: Having said that, let me briefly touch on the risks, and then recap the plan before moving on.

teaching.en: Asking who has never lost the thread during a digression is a rhetorical question, since nobody in the room expects a reply.
teaching.es: Preguntar quién no ha perdido nunca el hilo durante una digresión es una pregunta retórica, pues nadie en la sala espera respuesta.
teaching.explanationEs: La pregunta retórica no pide información: hace que el público piense y se incluya en la experiencia.
segments: Asking who has never lost the thread during a digression is
a rhetorical question, since nobody in the room expects a reply.
teaching.audioText: Asking who has never lost the thread during a digression is a rhetorical question, since nobody in the room expects a reply.

teaching.en: Skilled speakers conclude with a line that helps to drive the point home, one of the tricks of the trade.
teaching.es: Los oradores hábiles concluyen con una frase que ayuda a dejar clara la idea, uno de los trucos del oficio.
teaching.explanationEs: Drive the point home es una expresión fija; conclude con with introduce la frase de cierre.
segments: Skilled speakers conclude with a line that helps to drive
the point home, one of the tricks of the trade.
teaching.audioText: Skilled speakers conclude with a line that helps to drive the point home, one of the tricks of the trade.

teaching.en: Moving on closes one section, while a speaker who wants to conclude says to sum up to warn listeners that the final section has begun.
teaching.es: Moving on cierra una sección, mientras que quien quiere concluir dice to sum up para avisar al público de que empieza la última.
teaching.explanationEs: Cada señal tiene su lugar: las de cambio van en medio de la charla y las de cierre, al final.
segments: Moving on closes one section, while a speaker who wants to conclude says
to sum up to warn listeners that the final section has begun.
teaching.audioText: Moving on closes one section, while a speaker who wants to conclude says to sum up to warn listeners that the final section has begun.

prompt.es: Completa: «Dicho esto, no debemos ignorar el peligro que crean para los ciclistas.»

answer.text: Having said that

feedback.es: Having said that reconoce lo anterior (las ventajas) y contrasta con lo que sigue (el peligro).

hint.es: La señal debe reconocer lo dicho y luego contrastarlo.

origin.text: Cars are fast and cheap to run, and most drivers enjoy them. ___, we should not ignore the danger they create for cyclists.

prompt.es: Elige la señal que abre la frase final del resumen.

choices.text: Moving on to risks,
To sum up,
By the way,

feedback.es: Tras repasar costo, ventajas y riesgos, la frase final resume: To sum up anuncia el cierre; las otras dos abren otro punto.

hint.es: Pregúntate si la frase añade un punto nuevo o cierra los anteriores.

origin.text: We have examined the cost, the benefits and the risks of the scheme. ___ the plan deserves a trial, provided the council publishes its results.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Quién de nosotros no ha perdido nunca el hilo de una charla?»

answer.text: Who among us has never lost the thread of a talk

feedback.es: Who has never + participio forma la pregunta retórica: la respuesta implícita es que nadie.

hint.es: Empieza con Who; la respuesta implícita sería «nadie».

prompt.es: Completa: «Hizo más que cualquier dato por dejar clara la idea.»

answer.text: drive

feedback.es: Drive the point home es la colocación para dejar una idea clavada en la mente del público; hammer it home es una variante.

origin.text: The speaker ended with one photo. It did more than any statistic to ___ the point home, and people were still talking about it the next day.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cómo abre la oradora y qué hace con «Moving on»?

choices.text: A question that expects a reply, followed by a summary of earlier points.
A question that needs no answer, followed by the end of the talk.
A question that needs no answer, followed by a change of section.

feedback.es: La pregunta no espera respuesta (la oradora misma responde «I suspect we all have») y «Moving on» abre la sección siguiente.

origin.audio: Who has never arrived at a meeting without a plan? I suspect we all have. Moving on, let me briefly explain why preparation matters, and then I will recap the three habits that separate calm speakers from nervous ones.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada señal con lo que hace en la charla.

pairs: Having said that, the route is dangerous.

pairs.es: Matiza lo que se acaba de decir

pairs: Moving on to the budget, let us look at costs.

pairs.es: Cierra un punto y abre otro

pairs: By the same token, the second plan fails.

pairs.es: Aplica el mismo razonamiento a otro caso

pairs: Moreover, the tickets are cheap.

pairs.es: Añade otra razón al mismo punto

feedback.es: Cada señal tiene una función: matizar, cambiar de punto, extender un razonamiento o sumar una razón.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué función cumple «Moreover» en el discurso?

choices.text: It adds a second cause of forgetting to the one already given.
It opens a new section about a simple technique.
It marks the start of the speaker's closing summary.

feedback.es: «Moreover» suma un segundo motivo: además de no escuchar, casi nadie repite el nombre en voz alta.

origin.audio: Who has never forgotten a name the moment it was spoken? Nobody in this room, I suspect. First, I will explain why it happens: we are so busy preparing our own reply that we stop listening. Moreover, most of us never repeat the name aloud, which is the one habit that helps. Having said that, there is no need to feel guilty, because memory is not a skill we were ever trained to use. Moving on, let me briefly offer a simple technique, and then I will recap the whole idea in one sentence.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué actitud muestra el orador hacia quienes olvidan nombres?

choices.text: He is critical and blames listeners for making no effort to pay attention.
He is understanding: he treats it as a common habit, not a fault.
He is encouraging, but he thinks only trained public speakers can ever improve.

feedback.es: Explica el olvido como un hábito común y declara que no hay motivo de culpa: una actitud comprensiva, no acusadora.

origin.audio: Who has never forgotten a name the moment it was spoken? Nobody in this room, I suspect. First, I will explain why it happens: we are so busy preparing our own reply that we stop listening. Moreover, most of us never repeat the name aloud, which is the one habit that helps. Having said that, there is no need to feel guilty, because memory is not a skill we were ever trained to use. Moving on, let me briefly offer a simple technique, and then I will recap the whole idea in one sentence.

prompt.es: Completa: «Por la misma razón, nadie aprende a hablar memorizando un guion.»

answer.text: By

feedback.es: By the same token es la expresión fija para aplicar el mismo razonamiento a otro caso; no admite otra preposición.

origin.text: Nobody learns to swim by reading about it. ___ the same token, nobody learns to speak in public by learning a script.

prompt.es: ¿Por qué menciona el autor al orador que hace tres preguntas seguidas?

choices.text: To suggest that listeners dislike every kind of question put to them.
To complain about speakers who never take any questions from the audience.
To warn that a device loses its power if speakers use it too often.

feedback.es: El autor usa el ejemplo para advertir que un recurso eficaz pierde fuerza si se abusa de él.

origin.text: Advice columns love the rhetorical question. Who could possibly object to a little curiosity? Yet a speaker who asks three of them in a row sounds less like a guide than like a teacher giving an exam, and listeners soon notice that none of the questions is ever answered.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Pasando a otro punto, déjame tratar brevemente el presupuesto.»

answer.text: Moving on, let me briefly touch on the budget

feedback.es: Moving on abre la frase con coma; let me + verbo base introduce lo que el orador va a hacer.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué piensa la oradora del plan?

choices.text: She does not oppose it, but wants a second opinion first.
She welcomes it, and expects its weaknesses to disappear in time.
She rejects it, because cheap, quick plans always become expensive.

feedback.es: Reconoce las ventajas, pero «Having said that» introduce su reserva: no se opone, pero pide una segunda opinión antes de decidir.

origin.audio: The plan is cheap, and it is quick. Having said that, cheap plans have a habit of becoming expensive, and quick plans of becoming careless. So I am not against it. I simply want to see a second opinion before we sign anything.

prompt.es: Completa las tres señales: además, cambio de punto y cierre.

answer.text: Moreover | Moving on | To sum up
accepted: Moreover | Moving on | To sum up

feedback.es: Moreover suma una razón, Moving on abre otro punto y To sum up anuncia el cierre.

sentences: The scheme is cheap. ___, it is very quick to set up.
We know the costs now. ___, let us look at the risks.
We have seen three reasons. ___, the scheme is worth a trial.

es: Identificar en una charla escuchada el problema, la solución, la regla de tres, la llamada a la acción y el cierre que retoma el inicio.

vocabulary.es: guiño al inicio, retoma de lo dicho antes

teaching.en: Many talks follow one underlying structure: frame the problem, offer a solution, and end with a call to action.
teaching.es: Muchas charlas siguen una estructura de fondo: plantear el problema, ofrecer una solución y terminar con una llamada a la acción.
teaching.explanationEs: Underlying structure es el esqueleto que no se ve a primera vista pero organiza toda la charla.
segments: Many talks follow one underlying structure: frame the problem, offer
a solution, and end with a call to action.
teaching.audioText: Many talks follow one underlying structure: frame the problem, offer a solution, and end with a call to action.

teaching.en: To frame the problem, she showed a bin of perfectly good bread, a waste that no listener could easily forget.
teaching.es: Para plantear el problema, mostró un basurero con pan perfectamente bueno, un desperdicio que ningún oyente podía olvidar fácilmente.
teaching.explanationEs: Frame the problem significa presentar lo que va mal de modo que el público lo sienta como suyo.
segments: To frame the problem, she showed a bin of perfectly
good bread, a waste that no listener could easily forget.
teaching.audioText: To frame the problem, she showed a bin of perfectly good bread, a waste that no listener could easily forget.

teaching.en: The rule of three makes a list memorable because three parallel items feel complete, as in: plan, share and freeze.
teaching.es: La regla de tres hace memorable una lista porque tres elementos paralelos se sienten completos, como en: planificar, compartir y congelar.
teaching.explanationEs: Los tres elementos deben tener la misma forma gramatical (aquí, verbos en base) para que el ritmo funcione.
segments: The rule of three makes a list memorable because three
parallel items feel complete, as in: plan, share and freeze.
teaching.audioText: The rule of three makes a list memorable because three parallel items feel complete, as in: plan, share and freeze.

teaching.en: A simple solution is easier to repeat, and repetition is one way to reinforce the message after the talk ends.
teaching.es: Una solución sencilla es más fácil de repetir, y la repetición es una manera de reforzar el mensaje cuando termina la charla.
teaching.explanationEs: Reinforce the message describe el efecto de repetir o resumir la idea clave al final.
segments: A simple solution is easier to repeat, and repetition is
one way to reinforce the message after the talk ends.
teaching.audioText: A simple solution is easier to repeat, and repetition is one way to reinforce the message after the talk ends.

teaching.en: In the closing, a callback to the opening story lets the talk come full circle and leaves a lasting image.
teaching.es: En el cierre, un guiño a la historia inicial permite cerrar el círculo de la charla y deja una imagen duradera.
teaching.explanationEs: Come full circle: terminar donde se empezó, pero con un significado nuevo.
segments: In the closing, a callback to the opening story lets
the talk come full circle and leaves a lasting image.
teaching.audioText: In the closing, a callback to the opening story lets the talk come full circle and leaves a lasting image.

prompt.es: ¿Qué función cumple el fragmento dentro de la charla?

choices.text: It offers a solution based on sharing.
It returns to an image from the opening.
It frames the problem with a concrete figure.

feedback.es: La cifra concreta (miles de familias y pan bueno tirado) sirve para plantear lo que va mal: es el problema.

hint.es: Mira si el fragmento señala algo que va mal o algo que lo arregla.

origin.text: Every year, our town throws away enough bread to feed two thousand families, and most of it was still good to eat.

prompt.es: Completa: «Su última frase volvió al plato vacío inicial: la charla cerró el círculo.»

answer.text: circle

feedback.es: Come full circle es la expresión fija: la charla termina donde empezó, ahora con un significado nuevo.

hint.es: Es la figura geométrica de la expresión «come full ___».

origin.text: Her last sentence returned to the empty plate from the opening, so the talk came full ___.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Planifica con tiempo, cocina una vez y congela el resto.»

answer.text: Plan early, cook once and freeze the rest

feedback.es: Tres acciones paralelas, todas con verbo en base, forman una regla de tres rítmica y fácil de recordar.

hint.es: Hay tres acciones paralelas separadas por una coma y and.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿cómo plantea la oradora el problema?

choices.text: She starts with her own mistake, then shows how common it is.
She starts with a national scandal, then turns to her own kitchen.
She starts with her own mistake, then blames local shops for it.

feedback.es: Empieza con su propio pastel tirado (error personal) y amplía con lo que hacen las familias del pueblo.

origin.audio: Last month, I threw away a whole cake. I was not alone: every week, families in our town waste food worth thousands of dollars, and most of them never notice. The trouble is not a lack of care. It is habit.

prompt.es: ¿Por qué enumera la oradora exactamente tres acciones?

choices.text: Because three is the largest number of steps an audience can follow.
Because three parallel steps sound complete and are easy to remember.
Because each step answers one of three problems named earlier.

feedback.es: Tres elementos paralelos producen un ritmo completo y fácil de recordar; las otras dos opciones inventan una limitación o un dato que el texto no da.

origin.text: We can plan our meals. We can share what is left. We can freeze the rest. Three small steps, and the bin stays empty all week.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada fragmento con su función en la charla.

pairs: The trouble is that nobody sees the waste until it is in the bin.

pairs.es: Plantea el problema

pairs: Here is what works in my kitchen: plan, share and freeze.

pairs.es: Ofrece la solución

pairs: Clean, quiet and cheap: that is how a good bus should be.

pairs.es: Regla de tres

pairs: So, back to my cake: this time, it stays in the fridge.

pairs.es: Cierre que retoma el inicio

origin.audio: Imagine standing at a bus stop in the rain, watching the bus you needed drive away. That was my morning for three years. The trouble was not the buses; it was the gaps between them. So our neighbourhood tried something simple. We lent each other bicycles: one street, one shed, one key. Fast, free and friendly, it took us to work in twelve minutes. Today, the bus still leaves without me sometimes. But this morning, standing in the rain, I did not mind. I simply took a bicycle from the shed and set off.

prompt.es: Escribe el centro de una charla con inversión, regla de tres y pregunta retórica.

answer.text: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.
accepted: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.

Think about the last time you left a tap running. Why did you do it? Because nobody ever told you that it matters. Seldom have we been asked to think about water, and rarely do we wonder where it goes. Not until a dry summer arrives do most of us notice. So let me give you three rules that cost nothing. First, take shorter showers. Second, use the washing machine only when it is full. Third, fix every leak at once. Little did my neighbours believe that these three rules could save a thousand litres a month, yet that is exactly what happened on our street. At no point should we say that one person cannot make a difference, because every street is made of people like you and me. So when you go home tonight, look at your tap, and ask yourself one thing: what will I change first?

prompt.es: Escribe tu charla de cinco minutos: gancho, tres ideas, cierre y respuesta.

answer.text: Quick question: how many of you have ever lost a tennis match to a ten-year-old? I have, and it changed my life. Three years ago, I was a beginner at our neighbourhood tennis club, and I wanted to quit after one week. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, tennis taught me patience: I learned to wait before I move. Moreover, the club gave me friends who explained every mistake without laughing. Having said that, nobody ever made me feel small. Second, tennis changed how I deal with problems at work. Seldom have I felt so calm under pressure. Third, it costs almost nothing. You only need a ball and a friend. To sum up, be patient, be curious and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the ten-year-old? Last week, I beat her. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be good to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.
accepted: Quick question: how many of you have ever lost a tennis match to a ten-year-old? I have, and it changed my life. Three years ago, I was a beginner at our neighbourhood tennis club, and I wanted to quit after one week. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, tennis taught me patience: I learned to wait before I move. Moreover, the club gave me friends who explained every mistake without laughing. Having said that, nobody ever made me feel small. Second, tennis changed how I deal with problems at work. Seldom have I felt so calm under pressure. Third, it costs almost nothing. You only need a ball and a friend. To sum up, be patient, be curious and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the ten-year-old? Last week, I beat her. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be good to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.

Did you know that nine out of ten people who start a book club give up before the third meeting? I almost did. Last year I was a beginner, too shy to speak, and I told myself that nobody wanted my opinion. Today I will show you how I changed my mind. First, I chose a book that I loved, because passion is easier to share than duty. Moreover, I wrote down one question before every meeting. Second, I listened, and having said that, I also learned to disagree politely. Not only did the club improve my reading, but it also gave me the courage to speak in front of strangers. Third, I kept going even when the book was difficult. In conclusion, choose well, prepare one question and stay for the whole evening. That is my message. Good question, by the way: you asked whether you must be a fast reader to join. Not at all; slow readers often say the most interesting things.

origin.audio: Nine out of ten beginners quit a new sport in the first month, and I was nearly one of them. Three winters ago, I joined a rowing club at six in the morning, and for two weeks I hated every minute. First, I kept going because nobody laughed at my mistakes. Moreover, the club asked only that I turn up. Having said that, nothing was easy, and I never pretended otherwise. Seldom have I been so tired, and rarely have I been so proud. So if you are starting something new, find people who will wait for you.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué da a entender sobre la actitud del club hacia los principiantes?

choices.text: That it kept newcomers apart from its more experienced members.
That it expected every beginner to improve within a month.
That it valued commitment more than natural skill.

feedback.es: Nadie se reía de los errores y solo se pedía que se presentara: se valoraba la constancia por encima de la habilidad.

prompt.es: Completa: «Nadie esperaba una pregunta tan directa, pero ella supo responderla con calma.»

answer.text: field

feedback.es: Field a question es manejar con soltura una pregunta imprevista; handle o answer son alternativas defendibles.

origin.text: Nobody in the audience expected such a blunt question, but the speaker managed to ___ it calmly and then returned to her main point.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es el propósito principal de este consejo del entrenador?

choices.text: To persuade speakers to fix their structure but keep the wording flexible.
To warn speakers that a rehearsed talk is always a bad one.
To recommend that speakers write every word they plan to say.

feedback.es: Pide ensayar sin aprender cada palabra de memoria: conocer la estructura y dejar respirar el resto.

origin.text: Rehearse out loud, but do not learn every word by heart. A talk that is learned by heart sounds like a recording, and the first unexpected question will push it off course. Know your three ideas, know your first line, and let the rest breathe.

prompt.es: Ordena: «No fue hasta el cierre cuando reveló su idea final.»

answer.text: Not until the closing did she reveal her takeaway

feedback.es: Not until + expresión de tiempo invierte el orden: did va antes de she y reveal queda en base.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué da a entender la oradora sobre los nervios?

choices.text: That they disappear completely once she has enough practice.
That they are normal and can be managed with preparation.
That they reveal how little she has prepared for each talk.

feedback.es: Admite que siempre los siente, pero describe cómo los maneja: ensayo y recordar que el público está de su parte.

origin.audio: You asked whether I get nervous before a talk. Honestly, every single time. But I rehearse out loud, I pick up the pace when I feel my voice shake, and I remember that nobody in the room wants me to do badly.
